questions.q: A £100m fund makes {g}% (£{g}m) before fees. It charges 2% of the money managed, then 20% of the profit left. How much do investors keep, in £m?
questions.why: £{g}m − £2m = remaining profit; investors keep 80% of it: £{answer}m.

questions.q: An asset manager runs £{a}bn and charges an average 0.5% a year. What's its yearly fee income, in £m?
questions.why: 0.5% of £{a}bn = £{answer}m, whether or not its funds beat the market.

questions.q: Match each type of manager to what it does.
pairs: Picks investments to beat a benchmark
Uses shorting, leverage and derivatives for professional investors
Buys whole companies, improves them, sells them
questions.why: The buy side ranges from cheap index funds to complex, high-fee strategies.

options: A large part of the price is paid with borrowed money, repaid from the company's cash
The buyer uses only its own cash
The company is bought with shares from the stock market
questions.why: Borrowing magnifies the return on the fund's own money, and the risk.

questions.q: Hedge funds are always low-risk because they're hedged.
questions.why: Many use leverage, shorting and derivatives. The name describes a structure and tools, not safety.

questions.q: More debt in a buyout can turn a small fall in the company's value into a big loss on the fund's own money.
questions.why: Debt must be repaid first, so equity absorbs losses as well as gains in magnified form.

questions.q: Why are hedge funds usually limited to professional or wealthy investors?
options: They're riskier, less transparent and harder to sell out of
questions.why: Regulators restrict complex, high-risk, illiquid products for ordinary retail investors.

questions.q: Put the life of a private equity investment in order.
items: Buy a company with fund money plus debt
Improve the business and repay debt from its cash
Sell the company and share the profit
questions.why: Raise, buy, improve, sell. The performance fee (carry) comes from the profit at the end.

questions.q: What is stewardship by asset managers?
options: Using their votes and influence as shareholders to shape how companies are run
questions.why: Because they own so many shares, asset managers vote on directors, pay and deals, and engage with companies.

questions.q: Explain why a 2 and 20 fee structure sets a high bar for a fund to be worth it.

ideas.label: Fees take a big share of returns: 2% every year plus 20% of profits
So it must beat cheaper alternatives (like index funds) after fees, consistently

questions.model: The fund takes 2% of the money every year, whatever happens, plus 20% of profits, so a 10% gross return becomes about 6.4% for investors. To be worth it, it has to consistently beat cheap index funds by enough to cover those fees.
questions.why: High fees need high, reliable outperformance.

tests.answer: It takes 2% every year plus 20% of profits, so it has to beat cheap index funds after fees to be worth it.

questions.q: Explain how being paid a percentage of AUM can shape an asset manager's behaviour.

ideas.label: They earn more by gathering more money, even without beating the market
So investors should judge them on returns after fees

questions.model: Because fees rise with the money managed, a manager can earn more by gathering assets (through marketing or rising markets) than by beating the market. Investors should therefore judge managers on their returns after fees, compared with cheap alternatives.

tests.answer: They earn more by gathering more money even without beating the market, so judge them on returns after fees.
They want to attract more money.
